title.en: Malin Kundang: The Shipwrecked Son Who Cursed His Mother
title.zh: 馬林·昆當：詛咒母親而遭石化之子

region.en: Air Manis beach, Padang, West Sumatra
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘巴東·愛之水海灘

texts.period: Minangkabau oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Malin Kundang (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: A poor widow's son sails away from the Minangkabau coast and returns years later a rich captain, wed to a princess; passing his village, he denies his ragged, kneeling mother before his wife and crew — she curses him, and the storm that answers turns his golden ship to stone. The wreck-shape on the reef of Air Manis is still shown to travellers, with the footprint beside it.
summary.zh: 貧寡婦之子自米南加保海岸出海，多年後以富商船長之身歸來，且娶得公主；行經故村，竟當妻室水手之面否認跪地襤褸的老母——母親咒之，應咒的風暴將其金船化為石。愛之水海灘礁上之沉船形岩，至今為旅人指認，石旁猶有其足印。

sensitivity.note: The best-known Minangkabau moral legend (the ungrateful son); pilgrimage-site etiology.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Minangkabau oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
Malin Kundang is the Minangkabau world's great morality tale, told wherever a merantau people explains what leaving home owes to the mother who stayed.

BEGINNING: THE POOR HOUSE. In a fishing village on the Minangkabau coast a widow struggles to raise her only son, Malin Kundang. The boy, restless and ambitious, begs leave to go merantau — to seek his fortune abroad, as Minangkabau men must. He takes ship and is gone for years; his mother keeps his memory and her poverty, walking to the shore to watch for sails.

MIDDLE: THE DENIAL. Malin Kundang returns a rich captain in a golden ship, married to a princess, with a crew in livery. Ashamed of his origins before his new world, he passes his village without stopping; his mother, recognizing the son she begged heaven for, kneels before him and asks only to be acknowledged. Before wife, crew and passengers he denies her: he does not know this old woman, he says, ordering her pushed aside.

END: THE STORM AND THE STONE. The mother rises from the dust and curses her son: may he become a rock. As the ship puts out to sea, a black storm rises out of a clear sky; the golden ship is wrecked and turned to stone on the reef, the crew scattered, the captain flung onto the beach and frozen mid-crawl as stone. The rock on the shore of Air Manis is pointed out to this day as the ship-wreck shape, with the kneeling son beside it — and beside that, the legend insists, a hollow like a footprint.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) polices the merantau ethic: leaving is commanded by custom, but the umbilical debt cannot be defaulted; (2) makes matrilineal authority visible — the mother's curse, not the father's law, is the operative power; (3) etiologizes the reef-shapes of Air Manis beach as pilgrimage evidence; and (4) supplies the Malay world's best-known parallel to the filial-impiety petrification tales (Si Tanggang of the Peninsula). The tellings vary in detail but not in structure. In some versions the mother strikes the ship's rail with her hand, in others she kneels in the road; the curse may name the ship, the son, or both; and the petrification may catch the vessel at sea or the son crawling ashore. The Padang coast has consolidated the geography: the reef-shapes at Air Manis beach are pointed out as ship and kneeling man, and a hollow nearby serves the legend as the footprint of the son or of the mother who watched for his sails. The Minangkabau use of the tale is pedagogical: it is told to children preparing to merantau as the negative half of the custom's charter, the tale that explains why every departure must keep its line back to the mother's house. The Peninsula's Si Tanggang telling carries the same structure under another name, and the two traditions clearly descend from a shared Malay-world legend of the rich son who comes home too proud to kneel.
narrative.zh: 馬林·昆當乃米南加保世界之道德大傳——凡論『走他鄉』之民對留鄉之母負何債者皆述之。開篇：海濱漁村貧婦獨力撫養獨子馬林·昆當；少年懷志求去他鄉（merantau），乘船遠行多年，母親守貧守望，日日到岸邊看帆。中段：他以富船長之身歸來，金船、公主妻、華服水手；因恥於寒微，過家門而不入。母親認出跪求相認的兒子，在妻室水手面前遭他否認：『我不認識這老婦。』結尾：母親起身咒其為石；晴空裏風暴驟起，金船觸礁化石，船長被拋上海灘，爬行姿態凝固為石。愛之水海灘礁石至今被指為沉船之形、跪子之岩，石旁更有足印之凹。功能：規訓走他鄉之倫理——離鄉合俗，臍債不可賴；使母系權威可見——母咒而非父法為有效之力；釋愛之水海灘礁形為朝聖之證；並為馬來世界之『不孝石化』傳說（馬來半島之西·當當）供給最著名之平行文本。

functions: Policing the merantau ethic: the emigrant's umbilical debt to the mother cannot be defaulted
Matrilineal authority made visible — the mother's curse as operative power
Etiology of the reef-shapes of Air Manis beach, Padang
Malay-world parallel to the Si Tanggang petrification tale

title.en: The Buffalo That Won the War: How Minangkabau Got Its Name
title.zh: 贏得戰爭的水牛：米南加保之名由來

region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保腹地（巴加爾容）

texts.period: Minangkabau oral legend; recorded in early European accounts and local tradition

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the Menangkabau country; Minangkabau oral name-legend

summary.en: Invaded by a mighty Javanese army, the Minangkabau, too few to fight in the open, propose a single combat of buffaloes — and produce a starving calf with knives honed and bound to its tiny horns. The calf, seeking milk, gores the enemy's great fighting bull to death; the Javanese withdraw, and the land is named Minangkabau, 'the buffalo that won' (menang kerbau) — the origin myth of a people who call cleverness mightier than numbers.
summary.zh: 強大的爪哇軍入侵，米南加保人寡不敵眾，遂提議以水牛單挑定勝負——並牽出一頭挨餓的小牛，銳刃縛於其幼角。小牛尋乳本能，一觸即以角刃剖開敵方巨牛之腹；爪哇軍撤退，其地遂名『米南加保』——『得勝之牛』（menang kerbau）——一個以智勝於眾的民族的自敘神話。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology legend of the Minangkabau; the matrilineal people's self-image as clever underdogs.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Minangkabau oral name-legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The name-legend of Minangkabau is the charter story of the matrilineal highland people of West Sumatra, told with the buffalo that appears on their palace roofs — the bagonjong with its sweeping horn-like gables.

BEGINNING: THE INVASION. A great army out of Java under a mighty raja descends on the Minangkabau country; the highlanders, outnumbered past any hope in open battle, ask for terms — and the invader offers single combat of champions, in the form of a buffalo fight: his great bull against any beast the Minangkabau can produce.

MIDDLE: THE STARVING CALF. The Minangkabau produce a mere calf, starved for days and separated from its mother, with small sharp knives honed and lashed to its horns. On the field the enemy bull paws and bellows; the calf, a baby still, is let go — and runs straight at the great beast, nosing for milk.

END: THE NAME. The calf's bound blades rip the bull open in the first charge, and the fighting beast falls; the invader keeps the wager and withdraws his army. The land is named for its victory — Minangkabau, 'the buffalo that won' (menang kerbau) — and the people's houses are roofed with horns in memory of the calf that beat a bull.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) explains the name of the people and the horn-roofed architecture of their rumah gadang; (2) states the Minangkabau ethic that cleverness, preparation and mother-ties outweigh force; (3) encodes the memory of Javanese pressure on the highlands; and (4) links the matrilineal social order (mother-calf) to the land's safety. The legend's staging deserves its details: the wager of a single buffalo-fight replaces a war of annihilation, the calf's horns are armed in secret with small knives honed and lashed in place, and the animal's milk-seeking charge turns its hunger into the weapon. The story is told against the architecture as much as against the invader: the rumah gadang's sweeping horn-gables are read as the trophy of the calf's victory, so that every village skyline repeats the founding ruse. The historical layer beneath the legend is the memory of Javanese military pressure on the Sumatran highlands, which the Minangkabau chronicle traditions attach to Majapahit and to the line of Pagaruyung recorded in the Malay Annals; the buffalo contest is thus both name-charter and memory of survival — a people outnumbered, who won by preparing a weapon their opponent's strength could not anticipate.
narrative.zh: 米南加保之名源傳說是西蘇門答臘母系高原民族的憲章故事——其王宮屋頂之牛角形山牆即其象徵。開篇：爪哇大軍壓境；高原人力寡難戰，乃求和，侵略者提議以水牛單挑定輸贏。中段：米南加保人牽出一頭挨餓多日、與母分離的小牛，幼角上縛著磨利的尖刃。場上敵牛刨地吼叫；小牛被放開，逕直朝巨牛奔去——尋奶。結尾：小牛縛刃一觸即剖開巨牛之腹，戰牛倒地；侵略者守約撤軍。此地遂以『得勝之牛』（menang kerbau）為名，人民的房屋以牛角形屋頂紀念那頭戰勝公牛的小牛。功能：釋民族之名與大屋（rumah gadang）牛角頂之由來、立『智與備與母系勝於力』之倫理、銘記爪哇壓力之歷史記憶、並將母系秩序（母子相連）繫於土地之安。

functions: Explains the name Minangkabau ('the buffalo that won') and the horn-gabled rumah gadang roofs
States the ethic that cleverness and preparation outweigh force
Encodes the historical memory of Javanese military pressure on the highlands
Links the matrilineal social order to the land's safety

variants.summary: Later tellings name the invader as Majapahit and the victor's line as the Pagaruyung dynasty of the Malay Annals' Sang Sapurba.

title.en: Sabai nan Aluih: The Daughter Who Took Up the Gun
title.zh: 莎拜·南·阿魯伊：舉槍的女兒

region.en: Padang Tarab, Minangkabau highlands, West Sumatra
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保高原巴當·塔拉卜

source.work: The kaba of Sabai nan Aluih (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The famous beauty Sabai nan Aluih works the rice-fields with her aged father, the mild Mupo Rajo Nan Saludo; the quarrelsome great chief Rajo Babanding of Sungai Pagu demands her for a wife, and when the father resists the chief kills him. Sabai takes up her father's gun at the head of the young men of the valley, shoots the chief dead from a distance, refuses all marriage, and becomes the kaba's heroine of the daughter who ends the feud herself.
summary.zh: 著名美人莎拜·南·阿魯伊隨老父（溫和的穆波·拉佐·南·薩魯多）耕於田間；性暴的大酋長拉佐·巴班丁（蘇埃·帕古）索她為妻；老父抗拒，酋長竟殺之。莎拜於谷中青年之首拿起父親的獵槍，遠距一槍斃酋長；拒絕一切婚約，成為kaba傳說中親手了結仇怨的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Minangkabau heroine-romance; vengeance narrative treated as literature.

passages.text: Sabai nan Aluih works the rice-fields beside her aged father, Mupo Rajo Nan Saludo of Padang Tarab; the powerful chief Rajo Babanding demands her in marriage, and when the mild old father refuses him, the chief kills him at the field's edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Sabai nan Aluih; not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughter takes up her father's gun and leads the young men of the valley against Sungai Pagu; from long range she shoots Rajo Babanding dead, ends the feud with her own hand, and refuses every offer of marriage — the kaba's figure of the daughter who becomes her father's avenger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.

title.en: Anggun nan Tongga: The Kaba of the Mother and the Drifting Son
title.zh: 安貢·南·東加：母與漂泊之子之歌

region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保高原

source.work: The kaba of Anggun nan Tongga (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The noblewoman Anggun nan Tongga bears a son alone, sets him adrift on the river in a casket with royal tokens, and years later unknowingly takes the grown stranger as a husband — the Minangkabau kaba's great tragedy of separated kin, in which the recognition comes too late and the punishment falls on the house; the tale is told as a warning that a mother's secrecy can become a house's doom.
summary.zh: 貴婦安貢·南·東加獨自誕下一子，將其置於帶王家信物之木匣漂流於河；多年後，竟在不知情中嫁與這位成年的陌生人——米南加保kaba的大悲劇：至親離散、相認已遲、懲罰降於全家；故事警語曰：母親的隱瞞可成全家之禍。

sensitivity.note: Tragic kaba with an incest-recognition core; treated as literature, summarized without explicit detail.

passages.text: Anggun nan Tongga bears a son alone and hides the birth, setting the infant adrift in a casket bearing the tokens of his birth; the child is raised far away, knowing nothing of his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Anggun nan Tongga; not verbatim.

passages.text: Years later the grown stranger arrives at her house and is taken as a husband without recognition; when the tokens at last reveal the truth, the recognition has come too late, and the punishment of the hidden birth falls on the whole house — the kaba told as a warning against a mother's secrecy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.

title.en: Cindua Mato: The Journey to the Sky-Kingdom
title.zh: 金杜阿·馬托：上天國之旅

region.en: Minangkabau highlands and the sky-kingdom of the kaba
region.zh: 米南加保高原與kaba中之天國

source.work: The kaba of Cindua Mato (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The greatest Minangkabau kaba: the youth Cindua Mato ('ray of the sun'), sent up the sky-tree by the king to fetch the magical remedies of the sky-kingdom, climbs into heaven, wins the friendship of the sky-princesses, and carries down the cures that save his king — but the sky-world does not let its guests go freely, and the return costs the hero what heaven's princess loves in him. The kaba ends with the exchange fixed forever: Minangkabau's kings may have heaven's help, but heaven keeps its price.
summary.zh: 米南加保最偉大之kaba：青年金杜阿·馬托（『日光』）奉王命沿天樹而上，往取天國之仙藥；他攀入天界，贏得天國公主之誼，攜救王之藥而返——然天國不肯輕放其客，此行令英雄付出天國公主所愛之代價。kaba終章之約定永不改變：米南加保之王可得天之助，而天必收其價。

sensitivity.note: Sky-voyage kaba; the Minangkabau ascent narrative par excellence.

passages.text: Sent by his king to fetch the remedies that only the sky-kingdom keeps, the youth Cindua Mato climbs the sky-tree into heaven, where he wins the friendship of the sky-princesses and learns the cures of the upper world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Cindua Mato; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king is saved, but heaven does not release its guests freely: the kaba closes on the price heaven keeps from the hero, and on the standing bargain that Minangkabau's kings may call on the sky — if the sky may take its due.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.
